g.text: Warm audiences. Show the product, build desire and trust. (10 new formats)
N38 Behind the Build (Factory / Process Tour)
g.textArea:
What it is: A brand insider or a step-by-step sequence takes the viewer through where/how the product is made: opens on the finished product or the person on the factory/workshop floor, walks through materials, build and quality checks (often as numbered steps), and closes on the finished product in use or the reveal + brand card.

Why it works: Shows the craftsmanship and quality control behind the price, answering 'is it cheap junk / is it safe' objections with visible proof.

How to make one: 1) Get supplier/factory or workshop footage (ask your supplier for production-line clips) or film a rep in the warehouse. 2) Structure it as 3-4 steps: raw material > build > QC/packing, with one caption or line per step. 3) End on the finished product reveal or in use + offer.

Closest format already on the board: Pack An Order With Me (Fulfilment POV) - that shows packing a customer order; this shows manufacturing/quality of the product itself. Also unlike Founder Story, it is about the process, not the person's journey.

1 Eden Orchards

What it is: Shopper-POV video filmed inside a real, recognisable retailer: opens outside/at the shelf, the creator finds the product (or asks staff, who recommend it), shows the shelf, price tag and cart, then cuts home for close-ups and a 'grab it next time you're there / or online' close.

Why it works: Retail shelf presence borrows the store's credibility and signals 'this is a real mainstream brand', removing the 'random internet product' objection.

How to make one: 1) Only usable if the product is (or looks) stocked in a known store or a stockist boutique - film a POV walk to the shelf. 2) Show shelf, price tag, staff recommendation or the item going into the cart with captions on value. 3) Cut to home close-ups and end with 'in store or online, link below'.

Closest format already on the board: Product Demo / Day In The Life - here the setting (the retail aisle and the purchase moment) is the proof, not product use. Note: hard for pure dropshippers without retail placement.

What it is: The vertical frame is cut into 2-9 panels that all play at the same time for the whole ad: e.g. on-model 360 spin, macro fabric/detail loop, back view, several body types or several outfits, with a small brand/product label or one title tile ('Fall '26 is here', 'Stretchy jeans will change your life'); no VO or presenter, 6-15s.

Why it works: Shows fit, detail, movement and range in one glance with no edit for the eye to wait on, so it works as a richer catalog ad; best for apparel, underwear and anything where fit plus texture sells.

How to make one: 1) Shoot 3-4 short clips of the same product: on-model spin, back view, close-up texture/detail, and a second model or colourway. 2) Stack them as 3-4 horizontal panels (or a 3x3 grid for a collection) all looping at once, aligned to the same beat. 3) Add the brand + product name (or one headline tile) and keep it 6-15s with no VO.

Closest format already on the board: Try-On Haul [MOF] - a haul shows one creator trying pieces one after another with talking; here several silent views play at the same time in split panels, like a moving catalog page.

What it is: Opens with reverse psychology - 'Don't buy X', '3 reasons you SHOULDN'T buy X', 'Honestly, this isn't for everyone' - then runs a list of sarcastic or tongue-in-cheek disqualifiers ('if you're okay with blades that dull in months', 'if the pharmacy creams are working', 'you're just not that into glowing skin (said no one ever)'), each one secretly a benefit, before flipping to 'but if you want...' and closing on proof plus a guarantee/CTA.

Why it works: The 'don't buy' hook breaks ad blindness and makes the viewer qualify themselves in, so the pitch feels like honest filtering rather than selling; great for premium-priced products and markets tired of hype.

How to make one: 1) Open on a 'Don't buy [product] if...' / 'This isn't for everyone' line on the hero shot or a creator to camera. 2) List 3-5 disqualifiers that are really the pains your product solves (shown as captions, sticky notes or product demo shots, each with a wink). 3) Flip to 'But if you want [result]...', show one proof point or mechanism, and close on the guarantee and CTA.

Closest format already on the board: Myth Buster [TOF,MOF] - myth buster corrects a false belief; here the whole ad is framed as reasons NOT to buy, and each 'reason' is a disguised benefit before the flip.

g.text: N42 Pack My Bag (What's In My Bag)
g.textArea:
What it is: Hands (or a faceless torso) pack everyday essentials (phone, wallet, laptop, keys, lipstick, AirPods) into the bag one by one on a table or cafe bench, showing it swallows everything, then lift it onto the shoulder and close on the logo.

Why it works: Answers the main bag/organiser objection, 'will my stuff fit?', visually and in seconds, and the satisfying packing reads as native 'what's in my bag' content.

How to make one: 1) Lay the bag plus 6-8 recognisable daily essentials neatly around it on a clean surface or a lifestyle spot (cafe, desk). 2) Film overhead or chest height as hands drop items in one at a time, showing pockets/compartments; add one line of copy ('A work bag designed for more than the office'). 3) End with the packed bag zipped and lifted onto the shoulder, then logo.

Closest format already on the board: Product Demo Ads - a general demo shows features in use; this is one fixed beat (packing real daily essentials) that proves capacity and organisation.

g.text: N43 Partner POV (She Buys It For Him)
g.textArea:
What it is: A wife/girlfriend talks to camera (or narrates) about a men's product from her side: open on a line to other women ('ladies...', 'my husband used to...'), middle shows him using/wearing it as silent proof while she explains why she made him switch, close on the couple and a 'get it for him' CTA.

Why it works: Targets the woman who actually buys or gifts men's products, and her approval doubles as social proof for the man.

How to make one: 1) Cast a couple; she leads, he only appears in b-roll wearing/using the product. 2) Script: what she hated about his old version -> why she switched him -> what changed (looks, mood, confidence). 3) End with an affectionate couple shot and 'ladies, get this for your man'.

Closest format already on the board: Lesson From Others (Mentor Story) - third-person story too, but here the narrator is the buyer's partner and the ad is aimed at women buying for men.

g.text: N44 Prop Analogy Explainer (Physical Mechanism Demo)
g.textArea:
What it is: An expert in a white coat (or just hands) explains how the problem works using an everyday object as a stand-in for the body: opens on the prop and a hook ('nobody wants to be the short kid', 'double cleansing: scam?'), the middle acts the mechanism out on the prop (orange peel = pores, tube = urethra, pool noodle = growth plate, straw = blood vessel), and it closes with the product as the fix plus offer.

Why it works: A physical analogy makes an invisible mechanism instantly understandable and believable, and the odd prop is a pattern-interrupt hook; best for supplements, skincare and health devices.

How to make one: 1) Pick one cheap prop that mirrors the body part or problem (fruit for skin, hose for veins, sponge for gut lining). 2) Script 30-60s where every claim is shown on the prop: the problem happening, why common fixes fail, what your product's ingredient does. 3) Bring the product into frame next to the prop for the fix, then end with the offer.

Closest format already on the board: Fake Doctor / Animated Mechanism Explainer - Fake Doctor is a spoken endorsement and the Mechanism Explainer is animation; here the mechanism is acted out on a physical everyday prop, with or without a presenter.

g.text: N45 Styling Remix (One Piece, Many Looks)
g.textArea:
What it is: One hero item styled into several different outfits: opens with the item and a hook ('One skirt. Three lives', 'How I style my favourite boots'), cuts outfit by outfit with an occasion label each (school drop-off, lunch date, night out), and ends on 'which is your favourite?' or the product end card.

Why it works: Sells versatility and cost-per-wear, which kills the 'where would I even wear it' objection for a single mid-priced piece.

How to make one: 1) Pick one hero piece and plan 3-5 outfits around it for distinct occasions. 2) Film same spot, same framing; open on the item in hand + hook text, then quick-cut each look with an occasion label. 3) Close with 'Which is your favourite?' or the product name card and offer.

Closest format already on the board: Try-On Haul - a haul shows many different products; a remix keeps ONE product constant and changes everything around it.

What it is: Founder/rep with a lanyard filmed at an expo booth (banners, crowd) pitching and demoing the product live to camera, intercut with bold spec cards and a 'NEW' badge, closing on the rep summing up and the brand card.

Why it works: The expo setting signals a real, industry-recognised launch and makes a pitch feel like news coverage rather than an ad.

How to make one: 1) Film at a trade show, pop-up or market stall with branded backdrop - rep demos the product live. 2) Intercut 3-4 full-screen spec cards (key numbers) between demo shots, add a 'NEW' sticker. 3) End with the rep's one-line summary to camera + logo card.

Closest format already on the board: Stage Talk / Keynote Authority - no stage or audience lecture; it is a hands-on booth demo with spec cards, closer to a news segment from the show floor.

What it is: A horizontal, letterboxed excerpt from an independent long-form YouTube reviewer: often opens on a YouTube-style thumbnail hook, then the reviewer talks through and handles the product with screen recordings/specs, with a branded header bar, closing on 'see full review on YouTube' or a shop end card.

Why it works: An independent niche expert's real review carries authority no brand claim has; the YouTube look signals unsponsored, in-depth content.

How to make one: 1) Send product to niche YouTubers and license a 30-80s segment of their review. 2) Keep it horizontal with black bars, add a product-name header and burned-in captions; optional thumbnail-style opener. 3) Close with end card or 'full review on YouTube + discount code'.

Closest format already on the board: Celebrity Podcast Clip / UGC Reviews - this borrows a niche YouTube reviewer's long-form review (letterboxed), not a famous podcast or a vertical UGC creator.
